extracted.intended_audience: general readers, improv/comedy fans, television researchers and producers
extracted.subtask_description: Describes the format, production and common variant rules of the short-form improvisational comedy show Whose Line Is It Anyway?, including performer counts, game types, prompting methods, and how adaptations modify the format. Useful for understanding or producing similar TV improv shows.

rubrics_metrics.name: Panel of four performers
rubrics_metrics.description: The show consists of a panel of four performers who create characters, scenes, and songs on the spot.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The core production format uses four players performing short-form improvisation games; many international/adapted versions keep this four-player setup (examples in adaptations sections).

rubrics_metrics.name: Short-form improvisation games (many taken from theatresports)
rubrics_metrics.description: Performances are done in the style of short-form improvisation games, many taken from theatresports.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Games are typically brief, game-like structures rather than long-form narrative scenes. Examples and named games (e.g., 'Scenes From a Hat', 'Old Job New Job') are used across versions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Topics based on audience suggestions or predetermined prompts
rubrics_metrics.description: Topics for the games are based on either audience suggestions or predetermined prompts from the host.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prompts may be solicited live from the audience or prepared by the host/production; this prompt source shapes spontaneity and variety of scenes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Game-show framing with arbitrary points and a chosen winner
rubrics_metrics.description: The show takes the form of a game show, with the host arbitrarily assigning points and choosing a winner at the end of each episode.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Points are not meaningful competitively; the 'winner' designation is part of the entertainment framing rather than a rigorous scoring system.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adaptability of format for different audiences and markets
rubrics_metrics.description: International and spin-off versions adapt the format to target audiences and local tastes (e.g., children's version Sponk!, hip-hop variant Wild 'n Out, team-based variants).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adaptations may change contestant makeup (child performers), game selection, staging (rotating stage, props), musical emphasis, or competitive structure (two competing teams). Examples in the article: Sponk!, Wild 'n Out, Spinn, De Lama's, Quanta Categoria, etc.

rubrics_metrics.name: Continuity of production and cast across versions
rubrics_metrics.description: Multiple versions were produced by the same creators and have continuity of cast (e.g., performers from the British television show starred in the American series).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintaining production/performer continuity is noted as contributing to the show's identity; this can factor into authenticity when evaluating or producing adaptations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inclusion of guest hosts/guest-driven games and musical elements
rubrics_metrics.description: Some versions include guest hosts or guest-driven rules (e.g., a special guest suggests the rules of the last game), and the format includes improvised songs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Producers may invite guest stars to influence game choices or staging; musical games and guest interactions are recurring elements (Wild 'n Out features guest stars and hip-hop performances).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of a wide palette of succinct, repeatable game templates
rubrics_metrics.description: The show employs many repeatable game templates (short games with defined constraints) which can be re-used across episodes and adapted for local versions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Game templates allow consistent pacing and easy adaptation; the article lists that many games derive from established improvisation techniques and that adaptations both reuse and invent games.
